title: Intercontinental de Aviación 256
summary: Intercontinental de Aviación Flight 256, a 29-year-old Douglas DC-9-14, crashed into a marshy lagoon near María La Baja during approach to Cartagena. The aircraft descended below safe altitude and impacted terrain 56 km from the airport. Investigation determined the probable cause was incorrect altimeter setting, with altitude number 1 indicating 16200 ft on impact. Altitude number 2's lights did not work, preventing crew comparison and detection of the error. Contributing factors included lack of radar observation and insufficient training.
probable_cause: Wrong setting of the altimeter, resulting in altitude misjudgment and controlled flight into terrain. Contributing factors included lack of radar observation and crew loss of situational awareness during clear weather.

factors.evidence: altimeter number 1 indicated 16200 ft on impact and number 2's lights did not work
flight crew's loss of situational awareness due to clear weather relaxing them
airline's insufficient training of crews in this situation
plane impacted with the ground in a marshy lagoon near María La Baja

events.text: The aircraft departed El Dorado International Airport at 18:45 after being delayed by a failure on the previous flight.
The aircraft climbed to flight level 310 at 31000 feet altitude.
Air traffic control cleared the flight to descend to FL 140 and report when passing FL 200.
The aircraft passed through FL 200 at 19:33 after the descent was initiated.
The plane impacted with the ground in a marshy lagoon near María La Baja, 56 km from Cartagena Airport.

notes: sole survivor was 9-year-old girl with minor injuries

title: TAROM 371
summary: A TAROM Airbus A310 took off with the First Officer as pilot flying. The autothrottle reduced the left engine to idle, creating asymmetric thrust. The captain became incapacitated, and the First Officer, unfamiliar with Western-style attitude indicators and distracted by the captain's condition, failed to recognize the aircraft's severe left bank. The aircraft crashed near Balotești just 89 seconds after takeoff, killing all 60 people on board.
probable_cause: The autothrottle malfunction reduced the left engine to idle during climb. The captain became incapacitated, and the First Officer's confusion between Western and Soviet attitude indicator designs, combined with failure to recognize the deteriorating situation, led to loss of control.

factors.evidence: the plane's left engine moved itself back into idle, resulting in asymmetric thrust as the right engine remained at climb power
After Bătănoiu told First Officer Stoi he felt sick, he groaned then fell silent, apparently having lost consciousness
Stoi's inexperience with Western style ADIs led him to not know which way the plane was banking
the A310 was the first and only airplane that he had flown with a Western-style Attitude Direction Indicator
Preoccupied with trying to wake Bătănoiu, Stoi did not notice the rapidly increasing left roll
The aircraft crashed into the ground near Balotești

events.text: TAROM Flight 371 commenced take-off at 09:06:44 local time from runway 08R, with First Officer Stoi as the pilot flying
After Bătănoiu told First Officer Stoi he felt sick, he groaned then fell silent, apparently having lost consciousness
At 09:08:18, the engine thrust asymmetry reached its maximum value and the aircraft was banking severely to the left at an angle of 45 degrees
When Stoi realized the deteriorating situation, he reacted instinctively and attempted to engage the autopilot but disengaged seconds later
The aircraft crashed into the ground near Balotești at a speed of 324 kn, just 89 seconds after takeoff

title: Aviateca 901
summary: An Aviateca Boeing 737 on approach to El Salvador deviated from the standard approach due to heavy rain and thunderstorms. The crew intercepted the wrong ILS glide slope without briefing ATC of the deviation. ATC, unaware of the aircraft's true position, cleared a descent. The ground proximity warning system activated but too late. The aircraft crashed into the San Vicente volcano at 7,159 feet, killing all 65 on board.
probable_cause: The flight crew's lack of situational awareness in relation to the 7,159 foot San Vicente volcano obstruction and its decision to descend, combined with ineffective crew resource management.

the aircraft's ground proximity warning system activated, alerting the pilots that the aircraft was too close to the ground

title: Malaysia Airlines 2133
summary: The Fokker 50 descended too steeply and fast on approach to Tawau due to a late descent clearance. Despite warnings from the first officer about excessive speed, the captain maintained high speed. The aircraft touched down 3400 feet down the runway, bounced, and landed again at 4800 feet, leaving only 800 feet to stop. The aircraft overran the runway and crashed into a shanty town.
probable_cause: Captain's decision to continue approach with excessive speed and steep descent rate despite warnings, combined with late descent clearance, resulting in long landing and runway overrun. Airline fuel-saving and punctuality policies influenced the captain's decision to land despite insufficient stopping distance.

factors.evidence: Aircraft was high and fast for approach with 3000 ft/min descent at -13 degrees pitch angle
Aircraft speed well above normal for approach, captain maintained high speed despite first officer warnings
Aircraft touched down 3400 feet from runway threshold, bounced and final touchdown at 4800 feet down runway

events.text: Flight 2133 departed Kota Kinabalu 30 minutes late, weather at Tawau clear with 5600 ft runway available

title: Khabarovsk United Air Group 3949
summary: Khabarovsk United Air Group Flight 3949 crashed on 7 December 1995 during automated flight at 10600 m, killing all ninety-eight people aboard. The aircraft had instantaneously banked to the left shortly after taking off due to mechanical failure. Following maintenance, the aircraft had a tendency to roll to the left without any command from the pilots, but this issue was not rectified. The crew were unaware that the aircraft had banked to the right. Without proper monitoring and lack of alarm, the aircraft entered a heavy turn to the right, spiralling down without any possible recovery.
probable_cause: The crash was caused by a combination of mechanical failure, pilot error and design flaw. An unresolved mechanical issue causing roll to the left led the crew to conduct fuel transfer as a corrective action. The crew were unaware the aircraft had banked to the right, and without adequate monitoring systems or warnings, the aircraft entered an unrecoverable spiral descent.

factors.evidence: The aircraft had instantaneously banked to the left shortly after taking off due to mechanical failure.
Following maintenance, the aircraft had a tendency to roll to the left without any command from the pilots, and the issue was not rectified.
The crew were unaware that the aircraft had banked to the right.
The aircraft entered a heavy turn to the right, spiralling down without any possible recovery and crashed at high-speed.

events.text: The aircraft instantaneously banked to the left shortly after taking off due to mechanical failure.
The crew conducted a fuel transfer from the left tank to the right tank, creating imbalance towards the right.
The aircraft entered a heavy turn to the right, spiralling down.
The aircraft crashed into Bo-Dzhausa Mountain with a vertical speed of about 300 m/s and a pitch angle of about 70 degrees.

title: American Airlines 965
summary: During approach to Cali, the crew opted for a straight-in approach and mistakenly cleared all programmed approach waypoints from the FMS. The pilots selected the wrong radiobeacon identifier (R instead of ROZO), causing the autopilot to fly toward Bogotá. The aircraft descended into a valley north of Cali with ground proximity warning activated 12 seconds before impact. The crew attempted to climb clear, but fully extended speed brakes prevented adequate rate of climb, leading to stick shaker activation and terrain impact at 8,920 feet.
probable_cause: Navigational errors by the flight crew, specifically the selection of the wrong radiobeacon identifier and the failure to retract speed brakes during the escape maneuver.
